p: Muhammad Shaybani was a Shaybanid, a descendant of Shiban, son of Jochi Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan. His father was Budaq Sultan, one of the eleven sons of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, ruler of the Uzbek ulus, and his mother was Aq Quzi Begum. According to the historian Kamal ad-Din Binai, his father nicknamed him Shibägh, wormwood. Budaq Sultan was an educated man who had Persian works translated into Turkic, and Shaybani was fluent in both languages. He was fond of history in his youth, and in 1475 was presented with the Alexander Romance of Nizami Ganjavi.

He first appears leading 3,000 men in the army of the Timurid ruler of Samarkand, Sultan Ahmed Mirza. When Ahmed went to war with Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan over Tashkent, Shaybani secretly agreed with the Moghul khan to betray and plunder Ahmed's army, which he did at the Battle of the Chirciq River in 1488. Mahmud Khan rewarded him with Turkistan. There he oppressed the local Kazakhs, which led to a war between Moghulistan and the Kazakh Khanate that Moghulistan lost, while Shaybani's standing among the Uzbeks grew.

He ousted the Timurids from Samarkand in 1500, retook it in 1501, conquered Bukhara the same year and founded the Shaybanid dynasty of the Khanate of Bukhara. He fought successfully against Babur, later founder of the Mughal Empire, and married Babur's sister Khanzada Begum; Babur's freedom to leave Samarkand depended on his consent. He aligned himself with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II against the Shia Safavids. He patronised the Yemeni religious figure known as Mir-i Arab and wrote religious and philosophical works in Chagatai, among them the Bahr ul-Khudo of 1508. Raids on Kazakh lands in 1508–09 ended in a major defeat by Kasym Khan in 1510.

In 1510 Ismail I invaded western Khorasan. Shaybani had lost most of his cavalry in a campaign against the Hazaras, so he withdrew behind the walls of Merv. Ismail besieged the city for a month without result and then feigned a retreat. According to some sources the khan's emirs advised waiting for reinforcements, but his wife Aisha Sultan Khanum shamed the council into fighting. His army was surrounded by Ismail's 17,000 men and destroyed, and Shaybani was killed trying to escape, on 2 December 1510. Shaybani was succeeded by an uncle, a cousin and a brother, whose descendants ruled Bukhara until 1598 and Khwarezm until 1687.

notes: The article gives the capture of Samarkand as 1500 with a recapture in 1501; kept both.
The article spells his 1508 work both 'Bahr ul-Khudo' and 'Bahru'l-Huda'; I used the first.
The anecdote of Sheikh Mansour and the tablecloth, and the list of consorts, were left out.
The article does not say who held Samarkand between 1500 and 1501 (Babur, by its external links); I did not add it.
